parts.title: School Registration
parts.transcript: You will hear a number of different recordings and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Write all your answers in the listening question booklet. At the end of the test, you will be given ten minutes to transfer your answers to an answer sheet. Now turn to part one on page two of your question booklet. Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man looking for information on registering his child for school and a school district employee. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six. Good afternoon, Lemongrove School District. Hi, I'm calling for information on school registration. I think my son should attend one of the schools in your district. What grade will your son be entering? He just turned five. He'll be starting school this year. Oh, okay. Um, one moment, please. I'll get the information for kindergarten registration. Okay, thank you. Uh, can you give me your address? Yes, it's 7418 DeMarino Street. Okay, thanks. Yes, at that address, your child should attend Monterey Heights Elementary. Can you spell that, please? Yes, it's M-O-N-T-E-R-E-Y Heights. Great. So how do I register him? We have registration at each school site Monday through Thursday from 9 to 1. Oh, no, sorry, 1.30. You'll need to pick up a kindergarten registration packet from the school beforehand, though. It has all the forms you'll need to fill out. Can I pick up the packet anytime? Sure. The school office is usually open till 3.30 in the afternoons. Oh, no. I can't really get there that early. Well, the school has late office hours until 4 on Thursdays, or I think you can pick up a packet in the school library any day before 5. Oh, okay. I'll stop by there someday this week, then, before 5. Can you tell me what forms we'll need? I'm sure you need his immunization records. Yes, those, and we also need a general health history signed by your child's doctor, a form filled out by the dentist, emergency contact information, and a residency verification form with proof of residence. Oh, and an original birth certificate. Okay, that shouldn't be a problem. Can I ask one more question? Sure, go ahead. I was wondering about before and after school care. Do you provide transportation after school? No, unfortunately we don't. Parents or caregivers need to pick up the children. There is, however, an on-site licensed daycare for working parents who need after school care for their children. It's housed within the school grounds, and someone from the daycare will walk to the main school building to pick up your child each day. It's run by the City Youth Council and comes highly recommended. Can I get information about that as well? Yes, flyers and contact information will be included with your packet. Okay, thank you. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Oh, and one more thing. I saw a flyer recently for an introduction event for new students and parents. An open house, I think it was called. But I can't remember the date. Was it August 3rd? That must have been last year's flyer. We haven't put out information on this year's open house yet, but it'll probably be sometime in August. Ah, no, actually, it will be in July this year, since schools start a little early this year. Once your child is registered, you'll get all that information in the mail, and it'll be on the school website as well. Great. I'm assuming that during the open house, we get to tour the school and meet our child's teacher? Yes, and you will set up a time for kindergarten entrance testing as well. Wow, testing already. That starts early. Well, we want to make sure children are properly placed and qualified for special services, if necessary. Okay, I guess that makes sense. Oh, and the first day of school? The first day will be August 19. We start in the middle of the week to help with the adjustment, and for kindergartners, the first three days are half days, from 8 to 1230. Oh, okay. And then the next week, the regular schedule, 8 o'clock to 205, will be in force. Yes, and you can access the full school calendar of holidays and breaks on the school website. Oh, yeah, I've seen that. The website is very helpful. Thank you so much for your time. You're welcome, sir. That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a supervisor at Brightwater Adventure Park giving new summer employees some information about the park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Hello, everyone. Welcome to this information talk to help you during your first few days working at Brightwater Adventure Park. First, I'd like to give you this map of the site. It's important that you look round the whole site as soon as possible so that you can answer visitors' questions. I'll point out some of the main facilities now. Families often ask where the toilets that have baby-changing facilities are. Well, you see the big lake in the centre of the site. Follow the path that goes round to the west of that. Keep going until you come to the swimming pool and they're just after that on your left. Okay. If it's a really hot day, people buy lots of ice creams. There's an ice cream shop way over to the north of the site. From the station, follow the path that's lined with trees and you come to a sharp right bend. The shop's on the corner just before the train track crosses the path. Most people want to get a present to take home and will ask you where the gift shop is. You see the area called Young Fun and the road that that's on? There are some shops there and it's the last one you come to on that road. In fact, as you see, that road's a dead end. If people want a rest, recommend the film theatre. Let me point out where that is. See the central lake and you can see that the railway track runs very close to the lake. Okay. The film theatre's right next to the track, just inside the mega adventure zone. Got it? They show different films all day there on the three screens. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Now, some important information about rides. As you probably know, we've got a new ride called Flying Tigers. We already had lots of rides for older children, children taller than 1.5 metres, and we've got quite a few for children over 1.3 metres. But we wanted more rides for children who are over 1.1 metres. So Flying Tigers is for them. It's really exciting. Make sure you tell anyone going on the Hidden Cove ride that after about three minutes it suddenly goes dark. That can be scary if you're not expecting it. We want visitors to feel as if they're exploring deep underground. There's no water splash on that ride though, so getting wet's not an issue. If families want to have lunch, recommend the picnic area. It's nice and relaxing if the children have been running around all morning and they've used up lots of energy on the rides and play areas. There's a clown there between 11 and 2. He or she keeps the kids amused with jokes and stories. I'd like to tell you about a change to the programme for Saturday night. The barbecue won't finish until nine, so we're going to start the fireworks then instead of eight. Then there's a rock band that's very popular with teenagers. They'll play on the stage near the lake, not the one by the forest. We've got some special deals this month, so tell visitors that if they buy two soft drinks, they get a third one free. There's also 10% off tickets for another visit. And if they come back next month, they'll be able to get a photo of themselves at the park completely free. Now, just a small piece of advice to all you new employees. Do make sure you know where everything is. There are maps on boards on the path, so that'll help. Oh, and please keep a copy of the Adventure Park rules on you, so that if you see someone doing something that you think is dangerous or not acceptable, you can check. For example, some people want buses to wait for them if a family member's late, but the buses have to keep to their timetable. And if you have any problem... That is the end of part two. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part two.

parts.title: Translating ancient Mayan
parts.transcript: Part four. You will hear part of a history lecture about the translation of the language spoken by ancient Mayans who lived in Central America. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty. Thank you. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. When the Spanish arrived in Central America in the 1500s, they were surprised by the variety of Indian cultures there. One of the most interesting of the cultures, the Maya, had partially collapsed hundreds of years before. There were Mayan ruins everywhere, and they showed evidence of advanced engineering and a sophisticated tradition of writing. The Spanish thought that this written language of the Mayans which had survived could be a threat to the dominance of the Spanish language in the region, and so they tried to destroy all traces of it. Luckily, three books written in Mayan survived the destruction and were rediscovered in the 18th and 19th century in Europe. Each of the books contained a vast collection of ancient Mayan writings. All of these books were basically handbooks to be used by the priests. But for a long time, no one could read them. In the 19th and early 20th century, investigators managed to decode some numbers and some parts of the text which seemed to be on the subject of astronomy. But there were still large parts of the text they couldn't understand. Then, in the 1950s and 1960s, there were some breakthroughs. An amateur Mayan scholar called Heinrich Berlin, working in Mexico, decoded the first Mayan glyphs, which is the name given to the symbols that make up the Mayan script. He showed that these glyphs, in fact, represented famous cities that had once been a part of the Mayan Empire. He was then able to match these symbols with spoken words, because the name for somewhere famous doesn't usually change much over the centuries. So, by studying modern-day Mayan and listening to speakers of the evolved language, Berlin discovered how to say these symbols. Next to enter the picture was Yuri Norozov, a Soviet linguistics expert. He discovered that many Mayan glyphs actually played a phonetic role in the text. That means they stood for a sound, not just a single word as previously thought. So, two phonetic symbols together could, in fact, be one word, not two separate words. The door was open to crack the code. Beginning in the 1980s, several younger academics took a new approach. Unlike their forebears, who studied Mayans from a distance, this new generation immersed themselves by living among the Central American indigenous people, these young researchers came to have a deeper understanding of Mayan art and also a greater appreciation of the culture of the Mayans, both past and present, as well as of their religion. All this meant that there was a dramatic improvement in the quality and quantity of translation. The young academics discovered that many of the great events of Mayan history were recorded. In particular, many of the manuscripts described successes when kings fought wars with one another. But if the text was formal, the writing was not. The Mayan scribes who carved and painted the glyphs were often trying to be creative. So, there simply wasn't a standard system that scholars could refer to. But once the young academics got familiar with the style used by a particular Mayan writer, steady translations became possible. But, this type of translation takes a lot of time. Help was needed. Starting in 2003, one prominent scholar, David Stewart, looked for an online way for scholars and amateurs to post new inscriptions, refined translations, and discuss the subtleties of Mayan language. So, he started a blog that evolved into what is now the Maya Decipherment Project. Scholars in remote areas, who were often cut out of earlier research because of logistics, have become eager translation partners. Comments comments can be posted from anywhere in the world at high speed. It's estimated that there are more than 30 translators in 15 different countries currently at work studying and translating Maya script through the Maya Decipherment Project. Text by text, they are giving the modern world a better understanding of the lost Mayan world. The direction of this new understanding is that Mayans were not necessarily peaceful people who were wholly preoccupied with ceremony. This had been the general conclusion when scholarship was limited to the handbooks for priests that survived the Spanish. Thanks in part to the Maya Decipherment Project, new scholarship shows that the Mayans were interested in and wrote about the same topics as other ancient societies. That is the end of part four.
